how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Admin → General → Log Forwarding | Splunk: Settings → Data Inputs → filter by repository host source
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active log forwarding configuration or SIEM data input showing recent events from the repository.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the security operations or platform engineering team to confirm whether a log shipping agent is deployed on the repository host and actively forwarding to the SIEM. Request evidence such as a recent SIEM search showing repository audit events.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that a named SIEM (e.g., Splunk, Elastic) receives repository audit logs, with a sample query or dashboard demonstrating recent ingestion.

option_description: Records whether the currently installed version of the artifact repository software has one or more publicly disclosed CVEs in vulnerability databases such as NVD or OSV. Particularly relevant for CVEs affecting dependency resolution engines, metadata parsers, or REST API endpoints which are core to artifact repository operation.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires repository_software_not_patched when version_has_known_cve is true AND either patch_available is true or days_since_last_patch exceeds 30. Known CVEs in artifact repositories frequently target REST API endpoints (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application) or the dependency resolution engine (T1195.001 Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools), which can enable remote code execution, authentication bypass, or artifact poisoning without credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the installed Artifactory or Nexus version and query the NVD API for known CVEs affecting that specific version.
how_to_obtain.command: REPO_VERSION=$(curl -s https://<artifactory-host>/artifactory/api/system/version | jq -r '.version'); curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=Artifactory+${REPO_VERSION}&resultsPerPage=10" | jq '.vulnerabilities[].cve | {id: .id, description: .descriptions[0].value, severity: .metrics.cvssMetricV31[0].cvssData.baseSeverity}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON list of CVEs matching the installed version with severity scores; non-empty result indicates version_has_known_cve should be true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the OSV (Open Source Vulnerabilities) API to check the installed repository software version against the OSV database for known vulnerabilities.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X POST https://api.osv.dev/v1/query -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"version": "<repo-version>", "package": {"name": "artifactory", "ecosystem": "Maven"}}' | jq '.vulns[] | {id, summary, severity}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of vulnerability records for the installed version; empty array means no known CVEs in OSV.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory version endpoint to get the exact version string, then cross-reference with the vendor's security advisories page.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exact version string (e.g., 7.55.2) to use when checking JFrog Security Advisories at https://jfrog.com/security-advisories/

how_to_obtain.instruction: Visit the vendor security advisory page for JFrog (https://jfrog.com/security-advisories/) or Sonatype (https://support.sonatype.com/hc/en-us/sections/203012558) and search for advisories affecting the installed version number.
how_to_obtain.navigation: JFrog: https://jfrog.com/security-advisories/ | Sonatype: https://support.sonatype.com/hc/en-us → Security Advisories
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Advisory listings filtered to the installed version; presence of any advisory confirms version_has_known_cve is true.

option_description: Measures the elapsed time in days between the most recent software update or security patch applied to the artifact repository and the current assessment date. Used to quantify patch currency and identify repositories running stale software regardless of whether specific CVEs are known.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires repository_software_not_patched when version_has_known_cve is true AND days_since_last_patch exceeds 30. A high value in combination with known CVEs directly represents an exploitable window for T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) and T1195.001 (Compromise Software Dependencies). Even without known CVEs, repositories unpatched for extended periods are likely missing security hardening updates to dependency resolution engines and metadata parsers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the artifact repository container image's creation timestamp or the package installation date to calculate days since last patch.
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect <artifactory-container-name> --format '{{.Created}}' | xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo "Image created: {}"; echo "Days since: $(( ($(date +%s) - $(date -d "{}" +%s)) / 86400 ))"'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Container creation timestamp and calculated days elapsed; a value over 30 in combination with known CVEs triggers the policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For package-manager-installed Nexus or Artifactory, retrieve the installation or last-upgrade date from the package manager history.
how_to_obtain.command: rpm -qi artifactory 2>/dev/null | grep 'Install Date' || dpkg -l artifactory 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>2 {print $3}' || yum history list artifactory 2>/dev/null | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Installation date string; calculate difference from today: echo $(( ($(date +%s) - $(date -d '<install-date>' +%s)) / 86400 ))

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory system information endpoint to retrieve the version and cross-reference the release date with JFrog's release notes to calculate patch age.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:password https://<artifactory-host>/artifactory/api/system/version | jq -r '.version' | xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo "Installed version: {}"; echo "Check release date at: https://jfrog.com/help/r/jfrog-release-information/artifactory-release-notes"'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Installed version string; release date lookup on vendor site provides the reference date for calculating days_since_last_patch.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check container image labels or the application's VERSION file for build or release timestamps embedded in the deployment artifact.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OCI image labels including 'org.opencontainers.image.created' timestamp or 'build-date' label from which days elapsed can be computed.

option_description: Indicates whether the software vendor has published a patched release of the artifact repository software that addresses the specific CVEs present in the currently installed version. A true value means remediation is available and failure to apply constitutes an unacceptable risk.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires repository_software_not_patched specifically when version_has_known_cve is true AND patch_available is true. This combination represents the most actionable and indefensible risk state: known vulnerabilities exist, a fix is available, and it has not been applied. This directly enables T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) and T1195.001 (Compromise Software Dependencies), where attackers can exploit published PoC exploits for CVEs that the vendor has already patched in newer releases.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the JFrog releases API or Sonatype release feed to determine whether a version newer than the installed one exists that addresses known CVEs.
how_to_obtain.command: INSTALLED=$(curl -s -u admin:password https://<artifactory-host>/artifactory/api/system/version | jq -r '.version'); curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/jfrog/artifactory-oss/releases/latest | jq -r '.tag_name' | xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo "Installed: $INSTALLED"; echo "Latest: {}"; [ "$INSTALLED" != "{}" ] && echo "Patch available: true" || echo "Patch available: false"'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Comparison of installed version against latest release version; a mismatch where latest is newer indicates patch_available is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Visit the vendor's official release notes and security advisory pages to confirm whether a version addressing the identified CVEs has been released.
how_to_obtain.navigation: JFrog Artifactory: https://jfrog.com/help/r/jfrog-release-information/artifactory-release-notes | Sonatype Nexus: https://help.sonatype.com/repomanager3/product-information/release-notes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Release notes entry for a version newer than installed that lists a security fix referencing the CVE IDs affecting the current installation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the CVE entry in the NVD for the identified CVE to confirm whether the vendor has issued a fix and what version resolves it.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Version string representing the fixed version (versionEndIncluding or versionStartIncluding with vulnerable=false); if the installed version is lower, patch_available is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's patch management tracking system or ITSM tool (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira) to determine whether a patch ticket exists for the artifact repository, its current status, and whether the vendor has been confirmed to have released a fix.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Open or resolved patch ticket referencing the specific CVEs with vendor confirmation that a patched version is available for installation.

option_description: Identifies the network segment on which the artifact repository admin interface and artifact API are reachable — public internet, a flat internal network with broad host visibility, or a properly segmented/private network zone accessible only to authorized hosts.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'Network Exposure Without Segmentation' when network_exposure_scope is 'public_internet' or 'flat_internal' and neither ip_allowlist_enforced nor vpn_or_bastion_required is true. Public or flat exposure dramatically enlarges the attack surface for credential brute-forcing, CVE exploitation of the repository software itself, and unauthenticated artifact retrieval if anonymous access is misconfigured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to reach the repository admin port (default 8081 for Nexus, 8080/8443 for Artifactory, 80/443 for Harbor) from an external IP or a host in a different network segment using curl or nmap.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If ports are closed or filtered from public IPs and unrelated internal subnets, scope is 'segmented_private'. Open and responsive from public IPs indicates 'public_internet'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query cloud provider security groups or firewall rules to determine which source CIDRs can reach the repository ports.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=group-id,Values=<sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions' --output json | jq '.[] | select(.FromPort <= 8080 and .ToPort >= 8080)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IpRanges containing '0.0.0.0/0' indicates public_internet exposure. Broad RFC1918 ranges without subnet restriction indicate flat_internal.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Artifactory, navigate to Administration → Security → Network. In Harbor, navigate to Administration → Configuration → System Settings. Review any listed allowed IP ranges or proxy settings that indicate network placement.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration → Security → Network | Harbor: Administration → Configuration → System Settings | Nexus: Administration → System → Network
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of restricted CIDR allowlists or VPN-only notation indicates segmented_private; absence with broad access confirms flat_internal or public_internet.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the reverse proxy (nginx/HAProxy/Traefik) configuration fronting the repository to identify upstream listener addresses and any source IP ACLs applied.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines with 'allow 0.0.0.0/0' or no 'allow'/'deny' directives indicate unrestricted exposure; explicit CIDR allow lists followed by 'deny all' indicate segmented access.

option_description: Indicates whether an IP allowlist or CIDR-based restriction is actively configured and enforced on the repository admin interface and artifact API endpoints, ensuring only approved source addresses can connect.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'Network Exposure Without Segmentation' requires that when network_exposure_scope is 'public_internet' or 'flat_internal', at least one of ip_allowlist_enforced or vpn_or_bastion_required must be true to avoid triggering. Without an IP allowlist on a publicly or broadly reachable repository, any internet host can attempt authentication, exploit unpatched CVEs, or abuse misconfigured anonymous access. Default is false, meaning allowlisting must be explicitly verified.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Artifactory, navigate to Administration → Security → Network and inspect the 'Allowed IP Ranges' field. In Nexus Repository Manager, navigate to Administration → System → Network and check 'HTTP Request Settings' for IP filtering. In Harbor, check Administration → Configuration → Allowlist.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration → Security → Network → Allowed IP Ranges | Nexus: Administration → System → Network | Harbor: Administration → Configuration
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A populated list of CIDRs with a default-deny posture confirms ip_allowlist_enforced = true; an empty field or 'all' indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory REST API for the current network configuration and inspect the allowedIPRanges field.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Populated CIDR values indicate enforcement is configured. Empty output indicates no IP restriction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check cloud provider security group or WAF rules to determine if source IP restrictions are applied at the infrastructure layer independent of the application.
how_to_obtain.command: aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name <waf-acl-name> --scope REGIONAL --id <acl-id> | jq '.WebACL.Rules[] | select(.Name | test("ip-allowlist"))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A matching WAF rule with an IPSet condition referencing specific CIDRs confirms network-layer enforcement even if app-level config is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect firewall or reverse-proxy configuration files for explicit source IP restrictions applied to repository ports.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'allow 10.0.0.0/8; deny all;' confirm ip_allowlist_enforced = true. Only 'allow all' or no directives confirms false.

option_description: Indicates whether all access to the artifact repository admin interface and artifact API is routed through a VPN tunnel or bastion/jump host, preventing any direct network path from external or flat-network hosts to the repository.
security_impact: The Rego 'Network Exposure Without Segmentation' rule checks that when the repository is on 'public_internet' or 'flat_internal' segments, either ip_allowlist_enforced or vpn_or_bastion_required is true. A VPN or bastion requirement means even if the repository software has an exploitable vulnerability, attackers without VPN credentials cannot reach it. Default is false, so this must be actively confirmed through topology review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Disconnect from the corporate VPN and attempt to reach the repository admin interface and API from an external network. A successful connection without VPN indicates vpn_or_bastion_required = false.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection timeout or TCP RST when off-VPN confirms vpn_or_bastion_required = true. Successful TLS handshake from external network indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform or network engineering team to confirm whether the repository DNS name resolves to a private IP only accessible via VPN, or whether a split-horizon DNS forces VPN-only resolution.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Internal DNS resolves to RFC1918 address while public DNS returns NXDOMAIN or no answer, confirming VPN-only reachability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review VPN gateway or zero-trust network access (ZTNA) policy configuration to confirm the repository CIDR or hostname is in the protected resource list.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Repository IP or hostname present in AllowedIPs or protected resource policy confirms VPN routing is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the cloud provider's VPC routing tables and internet gateway associations to confirm whether the repository subnet has a direct internet route or only routes to a transit/VPN gateway.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Routes pointing to a VGW or TGW (vpn/transit gateway) instead of an IGW (internet gateway) confirm VPN-enforced access.

option_description: The total count of distinct permission scopes, roles, or access control groups defined across all artifact repositories. A value of 1 means a single permission scope governs all repositories regardless of their sensitivity level.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'Inadequate Repository Permission Segmentation' triggers when repository_permission_scopes_count equals 1 and sensitivity_tiers_represented has more than one entry. A single permission scope means a developer with access to a low-sensitivity dev repository inherits the same rights over production release artifacts, enabling lateral privilege abuse or accidental overwrites of release artifacts. Default is 1, representing the most common misconfiguration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory REST API to enumerate all defined permission targets and count distinct scopes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing the total number of permission targets. A value of 1 indicates a single shared scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Nexus Repository Manager, navigate to Administration → Security → Roles to count distinct repository-scoped roles. In Artifactory, navigate to Administration → Security → Permissions. In Harbor, navigate to Administration → Projects and review each project's member roles.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration → Security → Permissions | Nexus: Administration → Security → Roles | Harbor: Administration → Projects → Members
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of permission groups. Count the distinct repository-scoped groups; multiple groups named by repository type (release, dev, proxy) confirm segmentation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Nexus, query the REST API to list all roles and count those with repository-specific privilege assignments.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> http://<nexus-host>:8081/service/rest/v1/security/roles | jq '[.[] | select(.privileges[]? | test("repository"))] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer output. Values greater than 1 indicate multiple scoped roles. A value of 1 indicates a single role covering all repositories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If using Nexus with external config export or Artifactory with configuration-as-code (YAML backup), inspect the exported permissions/roles configuration file.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of permission elements. Count of 1 confirms a single global permission scope.

option_description: The list of sensitivity classifications assigned to the artifact repositories in use, such as 'release', 'internal-dev', 'third-party-proxy', or 'staging'. Used to determine whether multiple sensitivity tiers coexist that warrant distinct permission scopes.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'Inadequate Repository Permission Segmentation' evaluates whether count(sensitivity_tiers_represented) > 1, and if so, requires that repository_permission_scopes_count is not 1 and cross_tier_write_access_permitted is false. When multiple tiers exist — for example both 'release' and 'internal-dev' — but share a single permission scope, a compromised developer credential gains write access to production release artifacts, enabling silent artifact replacement attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the repository list in the artifact manager (Artifactory: Administration → Repositories → Repositories; Nexus: Administration → Repository → Repositories; Harbor: Projects list). Review repository names, descriptions, and tags to classify each by sensitivity tier.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration → Repositories → Repositories | Nexus: Administration → Repository → Repositories | Harbor: Projects (main navigation)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of repositories with names or labels indicating their purpose, e.g., 'libs-release-local', 'libs-snapshot-local', 'pypi-proxy', 'helm-staging'. Classify each into tiers: release, internal-dev, third-party-proxy, staging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory repository list API and group results by repository type (local, remote, virtual) and package type to derive sensitivity tiers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON grouped by local (internal), remote (proxy), and virtual (aggregated) types. Presence of both local release repos and remote proxy repos indicates multiple sensitivity tiers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Nexus, query the repository list API and extract repository names and formats to classify tiers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of repositories with format (maven2, npm, pypi) and type (hosted, proxy, group). Hosted repositories typically represent internal/release tiers; proxy repositories represent third-party-proxy tier.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DevOps or platform engineering team and request the repository inventory documentation showing each repository's intended purpose and sensitivity classification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented inventory classifying each repository. The set of unique sensitivity classes present constitutes the sensitivity_tiers_represented value.

option_description: Indicates whether any user, role, or service account that holds write permissions on a lower-sensitivity repository (e.g., internal-dev, staging) also holds write permissions on a higher-sensitivity repository (e.g., release) under the same or overlapping permission scope.
security_impact: The Rego 'Inadequate Repository Permission Segmentation' rule triggers when cross_tier_write_access_permitted is true and multiple sensitivity tiers exist. Cross-tier write access means a compromised developer account or CI token can overwrite production release artifacts without requiring escalation, enabling silent supply chain poisoning. This is the most direct path to artifact injection attacks in multi-tier repository environments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Artifactory, list all permission targets and check if any single group has deploy (write) privileges on both release-local and dev/snapshot-local repositories.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> https://<artifactory-host>/artifactory/api/v2/security/permissions | jq '.[] | select(.repositories[]? | test("release")) | select(.repositories[]? | test("snapshot|dev")) | .name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-empty output (permission target names) indicates a single permission scope grants write to both release and dev repositories, confirming cross_tier_write_access_permitted = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Artifactory, navigate to Administration → Security → Permissions. For each permission target, inspect the repositories listed and the privileges (Deploy, Delete) granted. Check whether any group appears with write access across both release and snapshot/dev repositories.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration → Security → Permissions → [select each permission] → Repositories tab
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If any permission target shows both 'libs-release-local' and 'libs-snapshot-local' in its repository list with Deploy privilege, cross_tier_write_access_permitted = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Nexus, query the REST API to retrieve all role privilege assignments and identify roles that have 'nx-repository-view-*-add' or 'nx-repository-view-*-edit' on both hosted-release and hosted-snapshot repositories.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> http://<nexus-host>:8081/service/rest/v1/security/roles | jq '[.[] | select(.privileges | map(test("release")) | any) | select(.privileges | map(test("snapshot")) | any) | .id]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of role IDs with cross-tier write privileges. Empty array confirms cross_tier_write_access_permitted = false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request a user-to-repository permission matrix from the platform team and verify whether any CI/CD service accounts or developer roles are listed with write access on both release and development repository columns.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matrix showing no overlap between write-access principals on release vs. dev tiers confirms cross_tier_write_access_permitted = false. Any overlap confirms true.

option_description: Controls whether the proxy cache repository validates artifact checksums (SHA-256, MD5) against the upstream registry's published checksum values before caching and serving the artifact to internal clients.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'Checksum Validation Disabled On Proxy Cache' triggers when proxy_cache_enabled is true and checksum_validation_enabled is not true. Without checksum validation, a cached artifact could be silently corrupted in transit, replaced via a cache poisoning attack, or tampered with on the storage backend, and clients would receive the modified artifact without any integrity signal. This is particularly dangerous for binary distributions and Helm charts where digest-based verification is not inherent in the protocol.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Artifactory, navigate to Administration → Repositories → Remote Repositories, select each proxy repository, and under the 'Advanced' tab verify the 'Retrieve Checksums and Validate' option is enabled. In Nexus, navigate to Administration → Repository → Repositories, select a proxy repository, and confirm 'Content Validation' is set to 'Strict' under the 'Proxy' tab.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration → Repositories → Remote Repositories → [repo] → Advanced → Retrieve Checksums and Validate | Nexus: Administration → Repository → Repositories → [proxy repo] → Proxy → Content Validation
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Checkbox enabled or dropdown set to 'Strict' confirms checksum_validation_enabled = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory REST API for a specific remote repository configuration and inspect the 'retrieveChecksumAndValidate' field.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'checksumValidation: true' confirms validation is enabled. 'false' or field absent confirms disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Nexus Repository Manager, query the REST API for each proxy repository and inspect the remoteStorage contentMaxAge and negative cache settings that affect validation behavior, then check the validation attribute.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'strictContentValidation: true' indicates content validation is active for cached proxy artifacts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Nexus installations with a config export, inspect the repository XML configuration for the proxy repository's checksum policy attribute.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON or properties file containing 'checksumPolicy: STRICT' or 'strictContentTypeValidation: true' confirms validation is enabled.

option_description: Indicates whether the repository is configured as a proxy, remote, or virtual/group repository type that fetches and caches artifacts from an upstream external registry, as opposed to a pure local hosted repository.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'Checksum Validation Disabled On Proxy Cache' only evaluates checksum validation when proxy_cache_enabled is true, because proxy caching introduces a distinct integrity attack surface. When this is true, the repository acts as a trust intermediary — artifacts flow from external registries through the cache to internal consumers. This intermediary position creates risk of dependency confusion, cache poisoning, and serving of tampered artifacts if checksum validation and proxy allow lists are not independently enforced. A proxy repository set to 'public_first' resolution order is also the precondition for the 'Dependency Confusion Via Proxy Routing' exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Artifactory, navigate to Administration → Repositories and check the 'Type' column. Repositories listed as 'Remote' or 'Virtual' with remote members are proxy caches. In Nexus, navigate to Administration → Repository → Repositories and check the 'Type' column for 'proxy' or 'group' entries.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration → Repositories → Repositories → Type column (Remote = proxy cache) | Nexus: Administration → Repository → Repositories → Type column (proxy = proxy cache)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Repositories of type 'Remote' (Artifactory) or 'proxy' (Nexus) confirm proxy_cache_enabled = true. 'Local' or 'hosted' only repositories confirm false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory API to list all repositories and filter for type 'REMOTE', which represents proxy cache configurations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of remote repositories. Non-empty array confirms at least one proxy cache is active. Empty array means no proxy repositories are configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Nexus, query the REST API and filter for repositories of type 'proxy' to identify all active proxy cache repositories.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> http://<nexus-host>:8081/service/rest/v1/repositories | jq '[.[] | select(.type == "proxy") | {name: .name, format: .format, url: .url}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of proxy-type repositories with their upstream URLs. Presence of entries confirms proxy_cache_enabled = true for those repositories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, inspect the registry configuration files for proxy cache project settings, which are configured at the project level with a 'proxy cache' flag.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> https://<harbor-host>/api/v2.0/projects?page_size=50 | jq '[.[] | select(.registry_id != null) | {name: .name, registry_id: .registry_id}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Projects with a non-null registry_id are proxy cache projects in Harbor, confirming proxy_cache_enabled = true for those projects.

option_description: Controls whether artifact retention or cleanup policies are defined and active for the repository, governing automatic removal of stale, outdated, or deprecated artifact versions based on age, count, or last-downloaded criteria.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags 'excessive_retention_without_cleanup_policies' when cleanup_policies_configured is false, meaning unbounded accumulation of old artifact versions — including those with known vulnerabilities — remains accessible to build pipelines. Stale artifacts may be silently re-consumed by CI/CD jobs without security review, and excessive retention can also obscure malicious artifacts hidden among legitimate historical versions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Nexus Repository Manager, navigate to Administration > Repository > Cleanup Policies and verify that at least one policy exists and is assigned to the target repository. In Artifactory, go to Administration > Artifact Cleanup and check for configured rules. In Harbor, navigate to the project, select Tag Retention, and verify rules are defined and enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Nexus: Administration > Repository > Cleanup Policies | Artifactory: Administration > Artifact Cleanup | Harbor: Project > Tag Retention
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one active cleanup or retention policy visible and assigned to the repository

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Nexus REST API to list all cleanup policies and verify one is attached to the target repository.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array with at least one cleanup policy entry showing criteria such as lastBlobUpdated or lastDownloaded thresholds

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Artifactory to retrieve artifact cleanup policy configuration via the API.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration block showing defined cleanup job schedules and criteria

how_to_obtain.instruction: For self-hosted Nexus, inspect the nexus configuration database or exported repository configuration YAML for cleanup policy assignments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: References to at least one named cleanup policy linked to repository definitions

typical_values: true (expected in mature production deployments with defined retention SLAs)

option_description: Represents the age in days of the oldest artifact version currently retained in the repository, computed from the artifact's creation or upload timestamp to the current date. Indicates how long artifacts accumulate without removal when no retention policy exists.
security_impact: The Rego policy for 'excessive_retention_without_cleanup_policies' escalates concern when cleanup_policies_configured is false AND oldest_artifact_age_days exceeds 365, confirming that artifacts are accumulating over extended periods. Artifacts older than one year are likely vulnerable versions, obsolete dependencies, or forgotten binaries that build pipelines could inadvertently consume, increasing supply chain risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Nexus REST API to find the oldest artifact in the repository by sorting components by creation date and returning the earliest timestamp.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ISO 8601 timestamp of the oldest artifact; compute difference from current date to get age in days

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Artifactory REST API to search for the artifact with the earliest created date and compute age from today.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Epoch millisecond or ISO timestamp of the oldest artifact in the repository

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, use the Harbor API to list all tags across all repositories within a project, sorted by push time, to identify the oldest artifact.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:password 'https://<harbor-host>/api/v2.0/projects/<project>/repositories' | jq '.[].name' | xargs -I{} curl -s -u admin:password 'https://<harbor-host>/api/v2.0/projects/<project>/repositories/{}/artifacts?sort=push_time&page_size=1' | jq '.[0].push_time'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Push time of the oldest artifact; compare to today's date using: echo $(( ($(date +%s) - $(date -d '<push_time>' +%s)) / 86400 )) days

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Nexus, browse the repository via Administration > Repositories > Browse, sort by Created date ascending, and note the timestamp of the first entry. In Artifactory, use the Artifacts panel with a search sorted by Created date. Compute the difference manually or with a date calculator.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Nexus: Browse > <repository> > Sort by Created ASC | Artifactory: Artifacts > Search > Sort by Created ASC
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Oldest artifact creation date visible at the top of the sorted artifact list

option_description: Controls whether automated monitoring or alerting is configured to track TLS certificate expiry for repository HTTPS endpoints, ensuring timely renewal before certificates expire and cause service disruption or insecure client fallback.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'tls_certificate_expiry_not_monitored' triggers when cert_expiry_monitoring_enabled is false AND either the certificate expires within 30 days OR client TLS verification is disabled. Without monitoring, an expired certificate goes undetected until clients begin failing or — worse — silently falling back to insecure modes such as insecureSkipTLSVerify, exposing artifact downloads to interception and tampering in transit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the operations or platform engineering team to determine whether a certificate monitoring tool (e.g., Prometheus blackbox_exporter, Datadog TLS check, Nagios ssl_cert plugin, or Grafana alerting) is configured with probes targeting repository HTTPS endpoints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation of a named monitoring tool with an active probe configured against the repository HTTPS URL, including an alert threshold (e.g., alert when <30 days remain)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Prometheus blackbox exporter configuration to verify an HTTPS probe targets the repository endpoint with TLS expiry checking enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A module entry with 'prober: http' and 'tls_config' targeting the repository hostname, plus a scrape config referencing that module

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a cron job or monitoring script is scheduled to test certificate expiry for the repository endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A scheduled cron entry invoking an ssl_cert check script against the repository hostname

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Datadog, PagerDuty, or alerting platform APIs for synthetic monitors or checks targeting the repository HTTPS endpoint for TLS validity.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'DD-API-KEY: <key>' -H 'DD-APPLICATION-KEY: <appkey>' 'https://api.datadoghq.com/api/v1/synthetics/tests' | jq '.tests[] | select(.config.request.url | contains("<repository-host>")) | {name, status, type}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A synthetic test of type 'ssl' or 'api' targeting the repository URL with an active status and alert configured

typical_values: false (common in self-hosted or legacy deployments without dedicated monitoring infrastructure)
true (expected in environments with Prometheus, Datadog, or Nagios managing infrastructure certificates)

option_description: Represents the number of days remaining before the TLS certificate serving the repository HTTPS endpoint expires. A value of 0 indicates the certificate is already expired, meaning clients will receive certificate errors and may fall back to insecure behavior.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'tls_certificate_expiry_not_monitored' triggers when days_until_cert_expiry is 30 or fewer and cert_expiry_monitoring_enabled is false, identifying the compounded risk of imminent expiry with no automated alerting. An expired certificate can cause clients configured with insecureSkipTLSVerify or ssl_verify=false to silently bypass TLS validation entirely, enabling man-in-the-middle interception of artifact downloads.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl to connect to the repository HTTPS endpoint and extract the certificate expiry date, then compute the number of days remaining.
how_to_obtain.command: echo | openssl s_client -connect <repository-host>:443 -servername <repository-host> 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates && echo "Days remaining: $(( ($(date -d "$(echo | openssl s_client -connect <repository-host>:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2)" +%s) - $(date +%s)) / 86400 ))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: notAfter field showing expiry date, followed by computed days remaining as a positive integer (or 0 if expired)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use curl to retrieve and display TLS certificate validity information for the repository endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing SSL certificate subject, issuer, and expiry date in the curl verbose output

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap with SSL scripts to enumerate certificate expiry details from the repository HTTPS port.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'not valid after' field showing the certificate expiry date; compute days from today manually or with date arithmetic

how_to_obtain.instruction: If using cert-manager in Kubernetes to manage the repository TLS certificate, query the certificate resource for its expiry status.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get certificate -n <namespace> <cert-name> -o jsonpath='{.status.notAfter}' && kubectl get certificaterequest -n <namespace> -o wide
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ISO 8601 notAfter timestamp from the certificate status; compute remaining days with date arithmetic

typical_values: 365 (certificates issued with standard 1-year validity, recently renewed)
730 (2-year certificates common with some internal CAs)

option_description: Indicates whether any repository client configurations — such as Helm, pip, conda, Maven, npm, or artifact downloader scripts — have TLS certificate verification explicitly disabled, allowing those clients to connect to the repository even when its certificate is invalid, expired, or self-signed.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'tls_certificate_expiry_not_monitored' triggers when client_tls_verification_disabled is true and cert_expiry_monitoring_enabled is false. Disabling TLS verification means clients cannot detect certificate substitution by a man-in-the-middle attacker, enabling interception and modification of artifact payloads in transit without any client-visible error. This is particularly dangerous in CI/CD pipelines where build tools pull dependencies automatically.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Helm repository configuration files for insecureSkipTLSVerify flags, pip configuration for ssl_verify settings, and conda configuration for ssl_verify options across pipeline agent home directories and CI/CD runner environments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any match indicates TLS verification is disabled; no output means verification is likely enabled across client configurations

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search CI/CD pipeline definition files (GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, Jenkinsfiles) for flags that disable TLS verification in artifact download or Helm commands.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any matching line confirms TLS verification is suppressed in pipeline artifact operations

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Maven settings.xml and Gradle build files for properties that disable SSL hostname verification when connecting to artifact repositories.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries such as <checkLatestSnapshots>false</checkLatestSnapshots> or custom SSLContext disabling validation

how_to_obtain.instruction: Audit npm configuration for strict-ssl disabled flags across user and project-level .npmrc files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File paths where strict-ssl=false is configured, confirming TLS verification is disabled for npm artifact operations

typical_values: false (expected secure default — TLS verification enabled)
true (common workaround for self-signed certs in dev/staging environments, dangerously propagated to production)

option_description: Controls whether automated backups are configured for the artifact repository storage layer, including scheduled snapshots of artifact blobs and metadata, storage volume replication, or backup jobs that produce recoverable copies of repository data.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'backup_and_recovery_not_configured' triggers immediately when backup_enabled is false, representing a single point of failure where ransomware encryption, accidental deletion, or storage hardware failure results in permanent loss of all build artifacts. Without backups, software delivery pipelines cannot be restored and release artifacts needed for rollback operations are unrecoverable, directly supporting the adversarial goal of inhibiting system recovery (MITRE T1490).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Nexus Repository Manager, navigate to Administration > System > Tasks and look for tasks of type 'Export databases for backup' or 'Backup blob store'. Verify the task is enabled and has a scheduled cron expression. In Artifactory, navigate to Administration > General > Backups and confirm at least one backup configuration is active with a defined schedule.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Nexus: Administration > System > Tasks | Artifactory: Administration > General > Backups
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active scheduled backup task with a valid cron expression and an enabled status indicator

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Nexus REST API to list all scheduled tasks and filter for backup-related tasks.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:password https://<nexus-host>/service/rest/v1/tasks | jq '.items[] | select(.type | test("backup|export"; "i")) | {id, name, type, enabled, nextRun}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON entries showing backup tasks with 'enabled: true' and a nextRun timestamp in the future

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for backup-related cron jobs or systemd timers on the host running the artifact repository that invoke snapshot, rsync, or cloud storage backup operations.
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'backup|snapshot|rsync|aws s3|gsutil|azcopy'; systemctl list-timers | grep -iE 'backup|snapshot'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active cron or systemd timer entries invoking a backup mechanism for repository storage

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Artifactory's system configuration file for backup definitions, or review Harbor's backup operator or Velero configuration if deployed on Kubernetes.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/artifactory/artifactory.config.import.xml | grep -A 10 '<backups>' ; kubectl get schedule -n <namespace> 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'harbor\|artifact'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A <backups> block with at least one enabled backup entry, or a Velero Schedule resource targeting the repository namespace

typical_values: false (common in ephemeral dev environments or newly deployed repositories without operational runbooks)
true (required in production environments with defined RTO/RPO objectives)

option_description: Indicates whether backup restoration from artifact repository backups has been successfully performed and validated within the current review period, confirming that backup data is intact, complete, and actually recoverable — not just that backup jobs are running.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'backup_and_recovery_not_configured' triggers when backup_enabled is true but backup_restoration_tested is false, recognizing that an untested backup provides false confidence. In the event of ransomware (T1485 Data Destruction) or storage failure, a backup that has never been verified may fail to restore due to corruption, incomplete data, or incompatible repository versions, resulting in permanent loss of production artifacts and making recovery as ineffective as having no backup at all.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the operations or platform engineering team to determine whether a documented restore drill has been performed within the past review period (typically 90 days or the last quarter). Request evidence such as a change management ticket, disaster recovery test report, or runbook execution log.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A dated record (ticket, report, or runbook execution log) confirming a successful end-to-end restore from backup to a test environment, with validation that artifacts were accessible post-restore

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review backup tool logs or restore operation logs for evidence of a test restore. Check Nexus backup task execution history, Artifactory backup logs, or cloud storage restore operations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries indicating a restore operation was performed, completed successfully, and artifacts were validated

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for documented disaster recovery runbooks or restore procedure scripts in the team's operational documentation repository, and verify the last execution date recorded in the script or runbook.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Script or documentation file with a modification date within the review period, indicating recent execution of a restore procedure

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review change management system (Jira, ServiceNow, PagerDuty post-mortems) for DR test tickets or restoration validation tasks associated with the artifact repository component.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jira: Search for issues with labels 'DR-test', 'backup-validation', or 'restore-drill' associated with the repository project | ServiceNow: Search change records for artifact repository backup testing
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A closed or resolved ticket with resolution notes confirming successful restoration test and artifact accessibility validation

typical_values: false (extremely common — backup jobs run but restoration is rarely tested in practice)
true (present in organizations with formal DR programs, SOC 2 or ISO 27001 compliance requirements)

option_description: Specifies the number of days that backup copies of artifact repository data are retained before automatic deletion. A value of 0 indicates no retention policy is set, meaning backups may be overwritten immediately or retained indefinitely without lifecycle management.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'backup_and_recovery_not_configured' triggers when backup_enabled is true but backup_retention_days equals 0, indicating that even though backup jobs run, no retention window is defined. Without a retention period, a ransomware attack (T1485) that encrypts repository data may corrupt all backup copies before the attack is detected, leaving no clean restore point. Conversely, indefinite retention without a policy wastes storage and may retain backup copies long enough to include artifacts with embedded secrets or deprecated vulnerable versions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Artifactory, navigate to Administration > General > Backups and review the 'Retention Period (days)' field for each backup configuration. In Nexus, check the backup task configuration for retention parameters. In Harbor with Velero, check the Schedule resource TTL setting.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Artifactory: Administration > General > Backups > [Backup Name] > Retention Period | Nexus: Administration > System > Tasks > [Backup Task] > Task properties
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric retention value in days (e.g., 30, 60, 90); a value of 0 or blank indicates no retention policy is set

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Artifactory system configuration API and extract backup retention settings.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://<artifactory-host>/artifactory/api/system/configuration' | python3 -c "import sys,re; c=sys.stdin.read(); print(re.findall(r'<retentionPeriodHours>(.*?)</retentionPeriodHours>', c))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Retention period in hours extracted from the system configuration; divide by 24 to convert to days (e.g., 720 hours = 30 days; 0 = no retention)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect cloud storage lifecycle policy configurations (AWS S3, GCS, Azure Blob) that govern backup object retention for the repository backup bucket.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket <backup-bucket-name> | jq '.Rules[] | {id: .ID, status: .Status, expiration: .Expiration}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A lifecycle rule with 'Status: Enabled' and an 'Expiration' block specifying 'Days' (e.g., 30); no rules or Days=0 confirms no retention policy

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-based deployments using Velero, inspect the Schedule resource TTL to determine backup retention duration.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get schedule -n velero -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.name | test("artifact|nexus|harbor|jfrog"; "i")) | {name: .metadata.name, ttl: .spec.template.ttl, schedule: .spec.schedule}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TTL field showing the backup retention duration in Go duration format (e.g., '720h0m0s' = 30 days); empty or missing TTL indicates no retention limit is configured

typical_values: 0 (default — no retention policy defined, common in misconfigured environments)
60-90 (typical enterprise standard aligned with audit and compliance requirements)
365 (extended retention for regulated industries with long-term artifact provenance requirements)
